title: Purple Biofortified Potato Offers New Weapon Against India's Hidden Hunger
excerpt: Kufri Jamunia, promoted by the Centre and developed by ICAR-CPRI, carries 3.22 mg of iron and 2.28 mg of zinc per 100 grams — several times a common potato — in a country where 57% of women and 67.1% of young children are anaemic.
body:
• Kufri Jamunia, a purple-fleshed biofortified potato released by ICAR-CPRI in 2024 and now being promoted by the Centre, contains 3.22 mg of iron and 2.28 mg of zinc per 100 grams — compared with 0.57 mg of iron and 0.28 mg of zinc in a common potato.
  • Its vitamin C is 42.75 mg per 100 grams versus 23.15 mg in a common potato, and its flesh carries 42.05 mg of anthocyanins per 100 grams.
  • The need is large in absolute terms: NFHS-5 found 57% of women aged 15-49 and 67.1% of children aged 6-59 months in India are anaemic.
  • For households, the utility is simple: this is not a supplement to buy — it is a familiar staple bred to carry more iron and zinc, yielding 32-35 tonnes per hectare for farmers in the North Indian plains.

A potato bred for nutrition, not just calories

India's Centre is promoting Kufri Jamunia, a biofortified purple potato developed by the Indian Council of Agricultural Research — Central Potato Research Institute (ICAR-CPRI), as one answer to hidden hunger: the condition where people eat enough calories but lack essential micronutrients such as iron, zinc and vitamin A.

Released in 2024, Kufri Jamunia is a medium-maturing table variety with dark purple skin and purple flesh, oblong tubers, shallow eyes and a mealy texture, according to the Press Information Bureau summary carried by Drishti IAS. Each plant produces 10-12 medium to large tubers.

The case for it rests on numbers, not colour alone. Figures shared by PIB and reported by Life and More put Kufri Jamunia at 42.75 mg of vitamin C per 100 grams against 23.15 mg in a common potato, 3.22 mg of iron against 0.57 mg, and 2.28 mg of zinc against 0.28 mg. In other words, per 100 grams it carries roughly five to six times the iron and about eight times the zinc of a conventional potato. Its flesh also contains 42.05 mg of anthocyanins per 100 grams — 80.66 mg in the skin — and about 161 micrograms of carotenoids per 100 grams.

How big is hidden hunger?

Hidden hunger is not a marginal problem. Data from the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5, 2019-21), widely cited in nutrition research, found anaemia in 57% of women aged 15-49, 67.1% of children aged 6-59 months and 59.1% of adolescent girls. Iron deficiency can impair cognitive development, weaken immunity and lower school performance, while zinc deficiency affects growth and immune function.

Biofortification works through the crop itself. Instead of adding nutrients after harvest or relying on tablets, breeders raise the nutrient density of a staple people already eat. Potatoes are a logical vehicle in India: they are eaten across regions and income groups, in curries, parathas, puris, snacks and processed foods.

Will farmers and consumers adopt it?

A nutrition variety fails if it yields poorly or cooks badly. Kufri Jamunia yields 32-35 tonnes per hectare under recommended practices, reaching 49 tonnes per hectare in station trials over 90 days, with nearly 90% of yield marketable. It has a 6-8 week dormancy period and good storage quality with low rottage and minimal weight loss, and it is recommended for the North Indian plains after multi-location trials.

It follows two earlier coloured varieties from ICAR-CPRI: Kufri Neelkanth, a purple-skinned variety released in 2018, and Kufri Manik, a red-skinned, yellow-fleshed variety released in 2021 that is also rich in iron and zinc. Kufri Jamunia goes further because the flesh itself is purple and its vitamin C, anthocyanin and carotenoid levels are higher than both predecessors.

In the kitchen, it is positioned as a direct substitute: traditional curries and parathas, snacks, halwa, and processed products including anthocyanin-rich potato flour for bakery items, soups and cookies.

What it can and cannot do

The honest limit matters. A more nutritious potato improves the nutrient content of meals, but nutrient content alone does not prove it will prevent or treat anaemia at population scale — that depends on how much is grown, how widely it replaces conventional potatoes, what else people eat, and whether iron is absorbed. No single crop closes a gap where 57 out of every 100 women are anaemic.

What Kufri Jamunia does offer is a low-behaviour-change intervention: no new habit, no supplement schedule, just a more nutrient-dense version of a food already on the plate. If seed supply and farmer adoption scale in the northern plains, its contribution will be measurable in diets first — and only then, over time, in deficiency rates.
